Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). A function $a\colon\mathbb N\to R$ has **finite support** when there is $N\in\mathbb N$ such that $a_i=0$ for every $i>N$. The **polynomial ring** $R[x]$ is the set of all finitely supported functions $a\colon\mathbb N\to R$.

For $a,b\in R[x]$ and $n\in\mathbb N$, define

$$ (a+b)_n:=a_n+b_n,\qquad (ab)_n:=\sum_{i+j=n}a_i b_j. $$

The convolution sum is a finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $R$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]). Write $0$ for the zero sequence, $1$ for the sequence with coefficient $1_R$ at index $0$ and zero elsewhere, and $x$ for the sequence with coefficient $1_R$ at index $1$ and zero elsewhere. The coefficient sequence supported at $0$ with value $r$ is denoted again by $r$, and a polynomial $a$ is written formally as $\sum_i a_i x^i$.

The closure of these operations and the commutative-ring axioms are established by [[lem-polynomial-operations-preserve-finite-support]] and [[thm-polynomial-ring-is-a-commutative-ring]].

For every commutative ring $R$, the coefficientwise addition and convolution multiplication of [[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]] make $R[x]$ a commutative ring. The constant-polynomial map $c\colon R\to R[x]$ is an injective unital ring homomorphism ([[def-ring-homomorphism]]).

The ideal generated by a subset and principal ideals.

For $S\subseteq R$, define $(S)$ to be the intersection of all two-sided ideals
of $R$ containing $S$.  This family is nonempty because it contains $R$, and
[[lem-ideal-criterion-and-intersections]] shows that $(S)$ is an ideal.  For
$a\in R$, the ideal $(\{a\})$ is written $(a)$ and is called **principal**.

The quotient ring $R/I$ with $(r+I)(s+I)=rs+I$.

Let $I\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$.  Since $I$ is an additive subgroup of the
abelian group $(R,+)$, its additive cosets form the quotient group $R/I$
([[def-quotient-group]], [[cor-subgroups-of-abelian-groups-are-normal]]).  Define

$$(r+I)(s+I):=rs+I.$$

The well-definedness and ring laws are established by
[[thm-quotient-ring-multiplication-well-defined-iff-ideal]] and
[[thm-quotient-ring-laws]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $g\in R[x]$ be monic. For every $f\in R[x]$ there are unique $q,r\in R[x]$ such that

$$ f=qg+r,\qquad r=0\ \text{or}\ \deg r<\deg g. $$

This includes the zero dividend and a constant monic divisor.

derivations.claim: Let $Q=R[X]/(G)$. By [F1] and [F2], $R[X]$ is a commutative polynomial ring, and [F3] makes $(G)$ a two-sided ideal and $Q$ a quotient ring. Since $G$ is monic of degree two, [F4] gives every class in $Q$ a representative $a(p)+b(p)X$ of degree at most one in $X$. If two such representatives define the same class, their difference is a multiple of $G$ and has degree less than two; uniqueness in [F4] forces the difference to be zero. Thus this representative is unique.

Construct the coefficient-substitution homomorphism R[X] to Z[x,x^-1] explicitly; it kills G and therefore induces a map from Q. In Q, X(X-p)=1, so the explicit Laurent substitution x to X and x^-1 to X-p gives the inverse map. The composites fix x and the generators p,X of Q, so the maps are inverse; step 1.1 then transfers the unique degree-at-most-one representative to the unique Laurent decomposition.

risk_review.notes: Read both proof steps and all five actual algebra suppliers. Monic division applies over Z[p] to G=X^2-pX-1, including zero and constant dividends. Multiples of G form exactly the principal ideal, so remainder uniqueness gives the rank-two normal form. Finite substitution kills G; X(X-p)=1 makes every negative Laurent power legitimate. The inverse composite sends p to X-(X-p)=p and fixes X; the other fixes x and its inverse. Existence and uniqueness hold for arbitrary finite support, including P=0, without AC. Read Carmi–Cohen v1 Appendix B.1 Proposition B.1, PDF pp.57–58; the local monic-division proof establishes the claim independently.
